passage_title: The Corner of Gorse and Water
passage:
[1] The photographs reached the Ardleigh Falls historical society in 1978 in four shoeboxes, and nobody could say when any of them had been taken. They were the working stock of a studio on Water Street that had photographed the town for sixty years — storefronts, flood damage, the mill gate at shift change — and had closed in 1961. A grandson of the photographer had written dates on some of the envelopes before he handed them over. Nessa Dunleavy, who took the collection on as a volunteer and stayed sixteen years, copied those dates into her notes and set them aside, on the ground that a man writing in 1977 about his grandfather’s business was working from the same photographs she was, and from memory besides.

[2] The usual way into an undated street photograph is to find something in the frame whose own date is known: a model of truck, a campaign poster, a hemline, a shop sign for a company that opened in one year and failed in another. Dunleavy used all of these and trusted none of them far, for a reason she repeated to anyone who asked. A thing in the frame tells you that the photograph cannot be older than the thing. It tells you nothing whatever about how much younger it might be. A truck sold new in 1923 is still on Water Street in 1938, and the poster for a lost election stays in a barbershop window until somebody scrapes it off. Evidence of that kind sets the early edge of a bracket and leaves the late edge standing open.

[3] So she hunted instead for disappearances. Anything removed — a chimney taken down, a watering trough pulled up when the paving went in, a wooden stair replaced by an iron one — closed the late edge, since a photograph showing the thing had to have been made before it went. Removals are less obliging than arrivals: a town records what it builds and rarely records what it loses. But the two kinds of evidence together, she wrote, “shut a door at each end,” and a bracket with two edges is a finding, where a bracket with one is a wish.

[4] Her most productive object was a tree. An elm stood at the corner of Gorse and Water, in the corner of hundreds of frames, and at some point it had lost a limb and begun to close over the wound. A tree closing a wound lays down a ridge of callus around the opening, a little more each year, and it never lays down less. Dunleavy could not say what year a given ridge belonged to. She could say, holding two photographs of that corner side by side, which was the earlier — and that was enough to put four hundred photographs into a line without knowing one date.

[5] Order is not date, and she spent as long converting the one into the other as she had spent building it. The tree warden’s ledgers gave the year the elm came down, which pinned the late end of the line. A glass plate in another collection, dated on its paper sleeve, showed the same corner clearly enough to be slotted into the ridge sequence, pinning a point near the middle. Two anchors on an ordered run date every photograph in it, with a spread that narrows near the anchors and widens between them, and Dunleavy published the spread.

[6] The method’s worst failure came of the same habit that made it work. She had ordered eleven photographs of the mill’s north wall by the progress of its repointing, assuming that mortar work advances across a wall and does not come back over itself. It came back: a section near the loading door had been repointed a second time, a decade after the first, and her line folded over on itself. What exposed the fold was not a document but the photographs. Two of them show the same man in the same coat on the same wet pavement, and her sequence had set eleven places between them.

[7] After that she qualified every date she printed, and printed her grounds beside it. A card in her files reads not “1931” but “1929–1934, by ridge at Gorse, between the plate and the trough,” which is unlovely and has one great virtue. When a mill payroll turned up in 1991 and moved the dated glass plate two years later than its sleeve had claimed, three hundred of her brackets moved with it, in an afternoon. Had she filed three hundred bare years, each would have had to be argued again from the beginning, and most would simply have stayed wrong.

[8] The dates in the Ardleigh Falls catalogue are still being adjusted, and that is the argument for the way she left them. What she built was not a set of answers but a structure in which one correction could travel, and the measure of such work is not how much survives untouched but how cheaply the rest can be found and moved.

was working from the same photographs she was, and from memory besides.
had no training in the archival work she had volunteered to take on.

It tells you nothing whatever about how much younger it might be. A truck sold new in 1923 is still on Water Street in 1938, and the poster for a lost election stays in a barbershop window until somebody scrapes it off. Evidence of that kind sets the early edge of a bracket and leaves the late edge standing open.

[3] So she hunted instead for disappearances. Anything removed — a chimney taken down, a watering trough pulled up when the paving went in, a wooden stair replaced by an iron one — closed the late edge, since a photograph showing the thing had to have been made before it went. Removals are less obliging than arrivals: a town records what it builds and rarely records what it loses. But the two kinds of evidence together, she wrote, “shut a door at each end,” and a bracket with two edges is a finding, where a bracket with one is a wish.

[4] Her most productive object was a tree. An elm stood at the corner of Gorse and Water, in the corner of hundreds of frames, and at some point it had lost a limb and begun to close over the wound. A tree closing a wound lays down a ridge of callus around the opening, a little more each year, and it never lays down less. Dunleavy could not say what year a given ridge belonged to. She could say, holding two photographs of that corner side by side, which was the earlier — and that was enough to put four hundred photographs into a line without knowing one date.

[5] Order is not date, and she spent as long converting the one into the other as she had spent building it. The tree warden’s ledgers gave the year the elm came down, which pinned the late end of the line. A glass plate in another collection, dated on its paper sleeve, showed the same corner clearly enough to be slotted into the ridge sequence, pinning a point near the middle. Two anchors on an ordered run date every photograph in it, with a spread that narrows near the anchors and widens between them, and Dunleavy published the spread.

[6] The method’s worst failure came of the same habit that made it work. She had ordered eleven photographs of the mill’s north wall by the progress of its repointing, assuming that mortar work advances across a wall and does not come back over itself. It came back: a section near the loading door had been repointed a second time, a decade after the first, and her line folded over on itself. What exposed the fold was not a document but the photographs. Two of them show the same man in the same coat on the same wet pavement, and her sequence had set eleven places between them.

[7] After that she qualified every date she printed, and printed her grounds beside it. A card in her files reads not “1931” but “1929–1934, by ridge at Gorse, between the plate and the trough,” which is unlovely and has one great virtue. When a mill payroll turned up in 1991 and moved the dated glass plate two years later than its sleeve had claimed, three hundred of her brackets moved with it, in an afternoon. Had she filed three hundred bare years, each would have had to be argued again from the beginning, and most would simply have stayed wrong.

[8] The dates in the Ardleigh Falls catalogue are still being adjusted, and that is the argument for the way she left them. What she built was not a set of answers but a structure in which one correction could travel, and the measure of such work is not how much survives untouched but how cheaply the rest can be found and moved.

prompt: The passage suggests that the elm’s ridge was a sounder basis for ordering photographs than the mill wall’s repointing was because the ridge:
choices: appeared in far more frames than the north wall, so its order covered more photographs.
could be ordered against the tree warden’s ledgers, while the mortar could not.
grows in one direction only, while mortar work can be done a second time.

correct_answer: grows in one direction only, while mortar work can be done a second time.
explanation: The fourth paragraph rests the tree on a one-way process — the callus grows “a little more each year, and it never lays down less” — while the sixth reports that the assumption that mortar work “does not come back over itself” was false, a section near the loading door having been repointed a decade later. How many frames an object appears in governs how much the order covers, not whether the order is right; the ledgers gave the finished run an anchor rather than a check on its order; and the passage never says how little mortar changes.
